title: Lipids: who gets a statin, how much, and what next

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which patients belong to a statin benefit group regardless of their calculated ten-year risk?
a: LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL or higher
questions.why: The fourth group is primary prevention chosen by the risk calculator. The other three are treated without needing a score.

questions.q: In primary prevention, above what ten-year ASCVD risk is a statin recommended?
questions.why: Between 5% and 7.5% a statin may be considered if risk enhancers are present. Above 20% the recommendation is a high-intensity statin.

questions.q: Which regimens count as high-intensity statin therapy?
questions.why: High intensity means an expected LDL fall of 50% or more. The three distractors are moderate intensity, in the 30% to 49% range.

questions.q: A 55-year-old has an LDL of 205 mg/dL and no other risk factors. What is the recommendation?
questions.a: A high-intensity statin now, without a risk calculation
d: Lifestyle change for six months, then recheck
questions.why: An LDL of 190 or more usually means familial hypercholesterolaemia, and the risk calculator underestimates lifelong exposure. Family members should be screened.

questions.q: In very high-risk ASCVD on a maximal statin, above what LDL is adding ezetimibe recommended?
questions.why: If LDL stays at 70 or above on statin plus ezetimibe, a PCSK9 inhibitor is the next step. Very high risk means multiple major events, or one event plus several high-risk conditions.

questions.q: After starting or changing a statin, when should lipids be rechecked?
questions.why: The recheck confirms the expected percentage fall and, quietly, whether the patient is taking it. After that, every 3 to 12 months.

questions.q: An intermediate-risk patient is unsure about a statin. A coronary artery calcium score comes back at zero. What does that support?
questions.a: Withholding the statin for now and reassessing in 5 to 10 years
questions.why: A score of zero lowers risk enough to defer treatment, except in smokers, diabetes, or a strong family history, where the statin still goes ahead.

questions.q: A patient on atorvastatin reports aching legs with a normal creatine kinase. What is the usual next step?
questions.a: Stop it, wait for symptoms to resolve, then rechallenge or try another statin at a lower dose
questions.why: Most statin-associated muscle symptoms are not true myopathy and many patients tolerate a rechallenge. True rhabdomyolysis, with a very high CK, is the exception.

questions.q: Which are risk enhancers that favour a statin when ten-year risk is borderline?
d: A single high blood pressure reading
questions.why: Others on the list are an LDL of 160 or more, chronic inflammatory disease, premature menopause, high lipoprotein(a), and persistent triglycerides of 175 or more.

questions.q: Above what triglyceride level does pancreatitis become the main concern?
questions.why: Below that, triglycerides are treated as an ASCVD risk marker through lifestyle and statins. Above it, a fibrate or omega-3 is added and alcohol and sugar are cut hard.

questions.q: Which statin dose is no longer recommended because of myopathy risk?
questions.why: Simvastatin also interacts with amlodipine, diltiazem and amiodarone, which cap its dose at 10 to 20 mg. The other three high doses are standard.

questions.q: A patient with diabetes aged 40 to 75 and no other risk factors. What intensity of statin is recommended?
d: High intensity only if LDL is over 190
questions.why: High intensity is reasonable when there are multiple ASCVD risk factors or the ten-year risk is 20% or more.
